items.stem: A patient slumps in the chair: unresponsive, gasping every 10 seconds, no definite pulse in 10 seconds.
options: Vasovagal faint: legs up and observe
why: Gasping with no definite pulse is cardiac arrest.
There is no pulse, so ventilation alone does not circulate blood.
Treating pressure first wastes the critical minute.

items.stem: An adult is not breathing but has a strong carotid pulse.
options: Respiratory arrest: open the airway and give about one breath every 6 seconds
why: Respiratory arrest with a pulse: ventilate (AHA suggests 10 breaths a minute) and recheck the pulse often.
Without breathing, arrest follows within minutes.

items.stem: A patient is pale and sweaty with a pressure of 76/40, responsive, breathing normally, pulse 104, an hour before the end of the session.
options: Deterioration with a pulse: lay flat, stop fluid removal, check the access and causes (Card 3)
why: Responsive with a pulse and breathing: deterioration, treated by cause.
Sinus tachycardia from low pressure is not treated with cardioversion.

items.stem: Heart rate 34, pressure 80/46, new confusion; the patient has a pulse.
options: Unstable bradycardia: atropine per protocol, then pacing or an infusion; treat causes
why: Low pressure and confusion are compromise.
Signs of compromise make it unstable.

items.stem: Heart rate 168, regular and narrow, pressure 124/78, alert, palpitations only.
options: Stable tachycardia: 12-lead ECG, vagal maneuvers, adenosine per protocol
why: Defibrillation is for pulseless or polymorphic VT.

items.stem: Monday, missed session, potassium 7.6 mmol/L, peaked T waves, alert with a pulse, connected.
options: Hyperkalemia with a pulse: calcium for ECG changes, shift, keep dialyzing

items.stem: A 7-year-old on dialysis is drowsy, breathing slowly, saturation 80%, heart rate falling from 120 to 70.
options: Respiratory failure: open the airway and bag-mask ventilate with oxygen
Wait for the heart rate to fall below 60
why: Children usually arrest from respiratory failure; ventilation breaks the chain.

items.stem: Which pathway for a 15-year-old with signs of puberty in cardiac arrest?
options: Adult BLS (30:2), with doses checked against weight and adult maximums
No CPR until weight is known

items.stem: Foam below the venous chamber, air alarm, the patient coughs and is breathless.
options: Stop the pump, clamp the venous line, do not return the blood, oxygen, lay flat
why: Sitting up may send air to the brain.

items.stem: Five minutes after connection: hives, wheeze, lip swelling, pressure 82/46.
options: Stop the pump, clamp, do not return; IM epinephrine per protocol
why: IV bolus of 1 mg is the arrest dose, dangerous with a pulse.

items.stem: Unresponsive, gasping, no pulse.
options: PEA: compressions and epinephrine as soon as feasible
why: Organized rhythm without a pulse is PEA.

items.stem: After CPR: strong carotid pulse, pressure 102/64.
options: ROSC: post-arrest care, pads stay on
why: A pulse and pressure confirm ROSC.

items.stem: Unresponsive, no pulse.
why: Chaotic trace with no pulse is VF.

items.stem: Talking, shivering under a blanket, pressure 130/80.
options: Artifact: check the patient and leads
why: A talking patient cannot be in VF.
Shocking a conscious patient is dangerous.

items.stem: Unresponsive, no pulse; flat line confirmed in two leads, gain up.
options: Asystole: CPR and epinephrine as soon as feasible
why: Routine pacing in arrest is not recommended.
items.findings: No pulse; confirmed in two leads

items.stem: Pulse present, pressure 70/40, confused.
options: Unstable VT with a pulse: synchronized cardioversion
why: Wide regular tachycardia with a pulse and compromise.
Adenosine only if regular, monomorphic and stable.

items.stem: Unresponsive, no pulse.
options: VT with a pulse: synchronized cardioversion
why: Pulseless VT is treated like VF.
Wide fast complexes are not sinus.

items.stem: Alert, pulse 62, missed Friday session.
options: Hyperkalemia with a pulse: protect, shift, dialyze
why: Peaked T waves in a missed-session patient with a pulse.
Tall narrow T waves are abnormal.

items.stem: Unresponsive, no pulse, missed two sessions.
options: Hyperkalemic arrest: CPR first; potassium treatment per unit protocol
why: A sine-wave pattern without a pulse is hyperkalemic arrest.
There is activity; cause is potassium.

items.stem: Pulse present, irregular, 150, pressure 84/50, chest discomfort.
options: Unstable AF: synchronized cardioversion (initial energy at least 200 J reasonable)

items.stem: Pulse 38, pressure 128/76, alert, no symptoms.
options: Stable bradycardia: monitor and find the cause
why: No compromise: monitor and look for causes such as potassium and drugs.
Not indicated, and not as a single 3 mg dose.

items.stem: Pulse present, alert, pressure 120/70.
options: Stable regular narrow tachycardia (SVT): vagal maneuver, adenosine per protocol
why: Too fast and no P waves.

items.stem: 8-year-old, pulse 52, mottled, weak pulses, despite good bag-mask ventilation with oxygen.
why: Under 60 with compromise despite effective oxygenated ventilation: CPR (PALS COR 1).
Hypoxic bradycardia does not respond to atropine alone.

items.stem: The monitor shows a wide, fast, regular rhythm. Before choosing treatment, what must you check?
why: Pulse decides arrest vs tachycardia algorithm.

items.stem: A patient is slumped and the monitor shows sinus rhythm at 80. What do you check first?
options: Breathing and a definite pulse together
why: Breathing and pulse place the patient.

items.stem: After an organized rhythm appears at a rhythm check, what confirms ROSC?
options: A definite pulse and a measurable blood pressure

items.stem: A tachycardia with a pulse at 160. Which assessment decides between cardioversion and drugs?
options: Signs of instability: low pressure, altered mental status, shock, chest pain, heart failure

items.stem: Before deciding to return the circuit blood in an arrest, what must the circuit nurse check?
options: Air, hemolysis, a severe reaction, or an open line end

items.stem: Before giving a pediatric epinephrine dose, what must be read aloud and confirmed?
options: Weight, dose in mg, volume in mL, and concentration

items.stem: Put the first actions of an arrest on the machine in order.
items.why: Recognize and call; compress; pads; shock a shockable rhythm; drugs when due. The circuit nurse stops fluid removal in parallel.

items.stem: Order the circuit nurse’s actions in an arrest with no circuit cause.
options: Make the access safe for drugs
Check for air, hemolysis, reaction, open line
Return the blood or clamp and disconnect
items.why: Stop fluid removal; check for a circuit cause; return or clamp; announce; prepare the access.

items.stem: Order the treatment of hyperkalemia with a pulse and ECG changes.
items.why: Protect, shift, remove, then monitor glucose after insulin.

items.stem: Order the steps for a child whose breathing is failing.
options: Compressions if HR stays under 60 with poor perfusion
Open the airway and bag-mask with oxygen
Call for help and the pediatric cart
Epinephrine if compromise persists after hypoxia is corrected
items.why: Call; ventilate; compress if needed; epinephrine if compromise persists.

items.stem: Order the first actions after ROSC.
options: Confirm pulse and pressure, pads on
Oxygen to 90 to 98% and MAP at least 65

items.stem: Which action is unsafe during an arrest on the machine?
options: Returning the blood after foam is seen in the venous line
Securing the venous needle for drugs
why: Returning blood after air pushes air in.

items.stem: Which is unsafe before a shock?
options: The circuit nurse holding the blood lines during the shock
Pads on dry skin away from the access arm
Disconnecting a machine not rated defibrillation-proof
why: Lines touch the patient and can carry current.

items.stem: Which is unsafe for a 20 kg child in arrest?
why: That is 2 mg, ten times the dose.

items.stem: Which is unsafe in a stable, connected patient with potassium 7.0 and peaked T waves?
options: Stopping dialysis and sending him home to return tomorrow
Insulin with glucose and glucose checks

items.stem: Which is unsafe for unstable polymorphic VT with a pulse?
why: The device may not synchronize to changing QRS shapes; use defibrillation.

items.stem: Which is unsafe in severe anaphylaxis on dialysis?
options: Pushing the 1 mg/mL ampule IV as a bolus
IM epinephrine into the outer thigh
why: A tenfold-concentration IV bolus with a pulse is dangerous.

items.stem: A patient with unstable bradycardia (HR 34, BP 78/40) becomes unresponsive and gasping; no pulse. Which algorithm now?
why: Pacing belongs to bradycardia with a pulse; routine pacing in arrest is not recommended.

items.stem: During PEA arrest, the next rhythm check shows VF.
Ten minutes after ROSC the patient loses the pulse again.
A stable SVT (BP 120/70) becomes BP 74/40 with confusion after adenosine.
A child’s heart rate rose with ventilation, then falls to 48 with poor perfusion despite good ventilation.
why: Under 60 with compromise despite ventilation: CPR.

items.stem: Hyperkalemia with a pulse (connected, dialyzing) progresses to a sine wave and no pulse.
options: Hyperkalemic arrest: CPR first, then potassium per protocol

items.stem: Recurrent short runs that stop on their own. Between runs: alert, pressure 112/68. 12-lead: QTc 590 ms; potassium 3.1.
options: Torsades with a pulse: magnesium may be considered, correct potassium, stop QT-prolonging drugs, pads on
why: Recurrent polymorphic VT with a long QT is torsades; magnesium may be considered (COR 2b).
Amiodarone lengthens the QT; it is for polymorphic VT with a normal QT.
Adenosine treats regular narrow tachycardia, not polymorphic VT.
Sync cannot lock on to twisting complexes; sustained polymorphic VT gets an unsynchronized shock.
items.findings: Runs stop by themselves; alert between runs; long QT

items.stem: The twisting rhythm does not stop.
options: Pulseless polymorphic VT: CPR and an unsynchronized shock now
Magnesium first, then shock if it persists
why: No pulse plus polymorphic VT is treated like VF: shock early.
Sync cannot find reliable R waves; the device may not fire.
The shock comes first; no routine magnesium in arrest (COR 3).
These are not sinus complexes, and there is no pulse.
